PRM_001.name: Foam Dressings (Absorbent)
PRM_001.indication: Moderate-to-heavy exudate wounds (PU Stage II\u2013IV, VLU, DFU). Hydrophilic inner layer absorbs; hydrophobic outer provides vapour/bacterial barrier and thermal insulation.
PRM_001.contraindications: Dry or necrotic wound beds (insufficient moisture donation).

PRM_002.name: Silicone-Border Foam Dressings
PRM_002.indication: Atraumatic adhesion for fragile skin. Prophylactic use over bony prominences to prevent pressure injuries. Reduces pain at dressing changes.

PRM_003.name: Alginate Dressings
PRM_003.indication: Highly absorbent seaweed-derived polysaccharide. Gels on contact with exudate. For deep cavities, moderate/heavy exudate, and minor haemostasis.
PRM_003.contraindications: Dry wounds (desiccates wound bed). Always requires a secondary dressing.

PRM_004.name: Hydrocolloid Dressings
PRM_004.indication: Occlusive, self-adhesive (CMC, gelatin, pectin) that gel on contact. For partial-thickness wounds, minor burns, low exudate. Promotes autolytic debridement.
PRM_004.contraindications: Clinically infected wounds (occlusive nature traps bacteria). Heavy exudate.

PRM_005.name: Hydrogel Dressings
PRM_005.indication: High water-content (70\u201390%) polymers that actively donate moisture to dry beds. Promotes autolytic debridement of dry eschar/slough. Cooling, pain-relieving.

PRM_006.name: Gelling Fibre Dressings
PRM_006.indication: Sodium CMC fibres that transform into cohesive gel. Vertical wicking minimises lateral fluid spread, preventing periwound maceration.

PRM_007.name: Transparent Film Dressings
PRM_007.indication: Thin adhesive membranes permeable to vapour/oxygen, impermeable to water/bacteria. For superficial, non-exuding wounds and Stage I PU friction protection.

PRM_008.name: Wound Contact Layers
PRM_008.indication: Porous perforated sheets (silicone mesh, lipido-colloid) placed directly on wound to protect fragile granulation tissue. Exudate passes through to secondary.
PRM_008.contraindications: None specific. Always requires a secondary dressing.

PRM_009.name: Silver Antimicrobial Dressings
PRM_009.indication: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial disrupting bacterial cell walls/DNA. For wounds with clinical signs of local infection or critical colonisation.
PRM_009.contraindications: Silver allergy. Must review after 2 weeks (stewardship).
PRM_009.guidelines: NICE ESMPB2; BNF; EWMA Antimicrobial Stewardship

PRM_010.name: Polyhexanide (PHMB) Dressings
PRM_010.indication: Broad-spectrum synthetic polymer active against MRSA/VRE and biofilms. No reported microbial resistance. For critically colonised/infected wounds.

PRM_011.name: Cadexomer Iodine Dressings
PRM_011.indication: Controlled slow-release iodine via cadexomer microspheres. Absorbs exudate while releasing iodine. For infected or sloughy chronic wounds with moderate exudate.
PRM_011.contraindications: Thyroid disorders. Pregnancy/lactation. Iodine allergy. Lithium therapy.

PRM_012.name: Povidone-Iodine Dressings
PRM_012.indication: Broad-spectrum antiseptic iodophor releasing free iodine. For superficial infected wounds, wound bed preparation. Non-absorbent formulations.
PRM_012.contraindications: Thyroid disorders. Pregnancy/lactation. Iodine allergy. Lithium therapy.

PRM_013.name: Medical-Grade Honey Dressings
PRM_013.indication: Gamma-irradiated Manuka honey providing osmotic autolytic debridement, malodour reduction, and antimicrobial action via low pH and hydrogen peroxide.
PRM_013.contraindications: Bee product allergy. Can cause stinging (concordance risk).

PRM_014.name: Charcoal Dressings (Odour-Absorbing)
PRM_014.indication: Adsorbs volatile malodorous compounds and bacteria. For malodorous, fungating, malignant, or heavily colonised chronic wounds.

PRM_015.name: DACC Antimicrobial Dressings
PRM_015.indication: Hydrophobic fatty acid coating irreversibly binds bacteria/fungi physically without chemical agents. Avoids AMR and cytotoxicity. For colonised/contaminated wounds.
PRM_015.guidelines: Int. Consensus on Antimicrobial Stewardship; EWMA

PRM_016.name: TLC-NOSF Dressings (Sucrose Octasulfate)
PRM_016.indication: Lipido-colloid layer inhibiting excess MMPs, rebalancing chronic wound milieu. Specifically recommended for diabetic foot and venous leg ulcers.

PRM_017.name: Protease-Modulating Dressings
PRM_017.indication: Composites (ORC/collagen) that gel on contact, binding and inactivating excess proteases (MMPs) and protecting endogenous growth factors. For stalled chronic wounds.
PRM_017.guidelines: Health Technology Wales TER235; WII Protease Consensus

PRM_018.name: Collagen Scaffold Dressings
PRM_018.indication: Animal-derived (bovine, porcine) structural scaffold supporting cellular migration, granulation, and epithelialisation for stalled chronic wounds.
PRM_018.guidelines: Adv Skin Wound Care (Wu S et al.); IWGDF 2023

PRM_019.name: Haemostatic Dressings (ORC / Collagen / Gelatin)
PRM_019.indication: Bioresorbable agents promoting clot formation. ORC (oxidised regenerated cellulose), collagen sponges, or gelatin for capillary/post-debridement bleeding control.

PRM_020.name: Saline Dressings
PRM_020.indication: Passive dressings for basic hydration of dry/necrotic wounds. Minimal therapeutic action.

PRM_021.name: Burn Dressings
PRM_021.indication: Specialised dressings for partial- and full-thickness thermal injuries. Includes biosynthetic membranes, silver-based burn sheets, silicone burn contact layers.
PRM_021.contraindications: Agent must trigger 'Refer to Burn Centre' advisory for full-thickness burns.

PRM_022.name: Hypochlorous Acid (HOCl) Dressings
PRM_022.indication: Endogenous antimicrobial in stable formulation. Broad-spectrum against bacteria, biofilms, fungi, viruses. Non-cytotoxic. For wound bed preparation and biofilm disruption.

PRM_023.name: Methylene Blue / Gentian Violet Dressings
PRM_023.indication: Polyurethane foam impregnated with MB/GV. Disrupts bacterial biofilms via photodynamic and direct antimicrobial mechanisms. For infected and biofilm-harbouring chronic wounds.
PRM_023.guidelines: Woo KY et al.; Int Wound J

SEC_001.name: Superabsorbent Polymer Dressings
SEC_001.indication: Polyacrylate polymers absorbing and locking massive exudate volumes. Prevent strike-through under compression. Reduce dressing change frequency.

SEC_002.name: Adhesive Island Dressings (Composites)
SEC_002.indication: Non-adherent contact layer + absorbent pad + adhesive border. For low-to-moderately exuding acute wounds and surgical incisions.
SEC_002.contraindications: High exudate (insufficient capacity). Fragile skin (adhesive border risk).

SEC_003.name: Non-Adherent Absorbent Pads
SEC_003.indication: Simple exudate absorption without wound bed adhesion. Basic secondary cover.

SEC_004.name: Foam Secondary Covers
SEC_004.indication: Thin, non-bordered foam sheets as secondary absorption over contact layers or alginates. Provides cushioning and fluid management without adhesive wound contact.

SEC_005.name: Gauze Dressings (Cotton / Non-Woven)
SEC_005.indication: Traditional low-cost packing and secondary absorption.
SEC_005.contraindications: Chronic pressure ulcers (NICE CG179 deprecation). Trauma on removal.

SEC_006.name: Paraffin Gauze (Tulle Gras)
SEC_006.indication: Open-weave gauze impregnated with soft paraffin to reduce adherence. For minor burns and skin graft donor sites.

FIX_001.name: Tubular Retention Bandages
FIX_001.indication: Seamless elasticated fabric for holding dressings without adhesives. Eliminates MARSI risks on fragile skin.

FIX_002.name: Silicone Adhesive Tapes
FIX_002.indication: Soft silicone for gentle atraumatic removal. For fragile, ageing, or corticosteroid-compromised skin. MARSI prevention.

FIX_003.name: Microporous Adhesive Tapes
FIX_003.indication: Breathable, hypoallergenic paper tapes for sensitive skin. Lower adhesion than zinc oxide.

FIX_004.name: Zinc Oxide Tapes
FIX_004.indication: Rigid, strong-adhesion, water-resistant tape. High MARSI risk. Reserved for robust skin only.

FIX_005.name: Cohesive Bandages
FIX_005.indication: Self-adherent elastic bandages sticking to themselves, not to skin/hair. Retention and light compression.

FIX_006.name: Conforming Bandages
FIX_006.indication: Lightweight non-rigid bandages moulding to body contours (joints/digits). Secures primary dressings without compression.

FIX_007.name: Wound Closure Strips
FIX_007.indication: Sterile adhesive strips for non-invasive closure of low-tension lacerations or surgical incisions.

FIX_008.name: Sub-Bandage Padding (Orthopaedic Wool)
FIX_008.indication: Padding layer beneath compression to protect bony prominences and redistribute mechanical pressure.

PWC_001.name: Liquid Skin Barrier Films
PWC_001.indication: Terpolymer/cyanoacrylate transparent waterproof coating on intact/compromised skin. Protects against MASD and caustic exudate.
PWC_001.contraindications: Open wounds (apply to periwound skin only).

PWC_002.name: Barrier Creams (Zinc / Dimethicone)
PWC_002.indication: Occlusive protective layer shielding periwound skin from heavy exudate or incontinence. Key for IAD prevention.

PWC_003.name: Silicone Adhesive Removers
PWC_003.indication: Silicone-based solutions painlessly dissolving medical adhesive bonds. MARSI prevention.

PWC_004.name: pH-Balanced Skin Cleansers
PWC_004.indication: Mild formulations (pH 4.0\u20136.8) removing wound debris and exudate without disrupting the skin acid mantle.

PWC_005.name: Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesives
PWC_005.indication: Flexible waterproof closure for low-tension lacerations and skin tears (ISTAP Types 1\u20132). Also serves as durable periwound protectant.
PWC_005.contraindications: High-tension wounds. Deep wounds requiring sutures.

PWC_006.name: Emollients (Skin Moisturisers)
PWC_006.indication: Lipid-replenishing creams maintaining skin hydration and barrier integrity around the wound. Prevents dryness, cracking, and breakdown.
PWC_006.guidelines: NICE CG179; EPUAP/NPIAP CPG; Dermatology best practice

PWC_007.name: Wound Irrigation Solutions
PWC_007.indication: Sterile saline, Ringer's lactate, or antimicrobial irrigants (PHMB, HOCl) for mechanical cleansing of wound bed and debris removal prior to dressing.
PWC_007.contraindications: Specific antimicrobial irrigant contraindications apply (e.g. PHMB hypersensitivity).
PWC_007.guidelines: IWII 2025; EWMA Wound Bed Preparation; Wound Hygiene guidance

THS_001.name: Standard NPWT (Pump-Based)
THS_001.indication: Active aspiration (\u221275 to \u2212125 mmHg) removing exudate, reducing bioburden, stimulating angiogenesis. For stalled Stage III/IV ulcers and complex surgical wounds.
THS_001.contraindications: Malignant wounds. Exposed vessels/organs. Untreated osteomyelitis.

THS_002.name: Single-Use NPWT (Disposable)
THS_002.indication: Canister-free portable NPWT via evaporation. Primarily for closed surgical incisions in high-risk patients to prevent SSIs.
THS_002.contraindications: Open wounds with high exudate (insufficient capacity).

THS_003.name: NPWT with Instillation (NPWTi-d)
THS_003.indication: Standard NPWT + automated cyclical instillation of topical solutions (saline, PHMB) with dwell time. For highly contaminated wounds.

THS_004.name: Multi-Layer Compression Systems
THS_004.indication: Gold standard VLU treatment (ABPI \u2265 0.8). Multi-component systems delivering sustained 35\u201340 mmHg at ankle to reverse venous hypertension.
THS_004.contraindications: ABPI < 0.5 (arterial disease). Uncompensated heart failure. DVT.

THS_005.name: Short-Stretch Compression Bandages
THS_005.indication: Inelastic compression: high working pressure, low resting pressure. For VLUs and mixed arteriovenous disease.

THS_006.name: Two-Layer Compression Systems
THS_006.indication: Simplified systems achieving 30\u201340 mmHg with reduced bulk. Faster application, improved patient concordance.

THS_007.name: Adjustable Compression Wraps
THS_007.indication: Inelastic Velcro-strap devices self-applicable by patients. Comparable VLU healing to short-stretch. For patients with limited dexterity.

THS_008.name: Compression Hosiery (Class 2/3)
THS_008.indication: Long-term maintenance therapy post-VLU closure to prevent recurrence.

THS_009.name: Intermittent Pneumatic Compression
THS_009.indication: Mechanical leg sleeves enhancing venous return. For patients who cannot tolerate bandaging or have restricted mobility.

THS_010.name: Larval (Maggot) Debridement
THS_010.indication: Sterile Lucilia sericata larvae selectively debriding necrotic tissue. Active against MRSA. When surgical debridement is contraindicated.
THS_010.contraindications: Patients near major blood vessels. Extreme aversion (concordance).

THS_011.name: Enzymatic Debridement Agents
THS_011.indication: Collagenase or bromelain selectively hydrolysing denatured collagen anchoring necrotic tissue. For ulcers and severe burns.
THS_011.contraindications: Clean granulating wounds. Regional availability varies (collagenase mainly US; bromelain EU).

THS_012.name: Mechanical Debridement Pads
THS_012.indication: Monofilament polyester pads for gentle, rapid removal of slough and hyperkeratosis at the bedside.

THS_013.name: Ultrasonic / Hydrosurgical Debridement
THS_013.indication: Low-frequency ultrasound devices or high-pressure waterjet systems for selective, precise debridement while preserving viable tissue.
THS_013.guidelines: EWMA Debridement Document; NICE interventional procedures

THS_014.name: Electrical Stimulation Therapy
THS_014.indication: Low-frequency electrical current promoting fibroblast migration in recalcitrant Stage II+ pressure injuries.
THS_014.contraindications: Pacemakers. Malignant wounds. Over metallic implants.

THS_015.name: Topical Oxygen Therapy
THS_015.indication: Delivers oxygen directly to wound surface to address local hypoxia. For non-healing DFU after 4\u20136 weeks of standard care.

THS_016.name: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)
THS_016.indication: Systemic 100% oxygen at elevated pressure (1.5\u20133 ATA). Enhances tissue oxygenation, fibroblast proliferation, angiogenesis in ischaemic wounds.

THS_017.name: Acellular Dermal Matrices
THS_017.indication: Biological scaffold for cellular invasion and neovascularisation in full-thickness soft-tissue defects.
THS_017.guidelines: WII Skin Substitutes Consensus; Scars Burn Heal

THS_018.name: Cellular / Bioengineered Skin Substitutes
THS_018.indication: Living or tissue-engineered constructs providing growth factors, ECM, and/or living cells. For chronic full-thickness wounds failing standard care.
THS_018.contraindications: Active infection. Cost and availability constraints.

THS_019.name: Autologous Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP)
THS_019.indication: Blood-derived concentrate with supraphysiological growth factors applied topically to chronic wounds.

THS_020.name: Non-Removable Offloading Devices (TCC / Irremovable Walker)
THS_020.indication: Gold-standard offloading for plantar neuropathic DFU. Total contact cast or irremovable walker redistributing plantar pressure.
THS_020.contraindications: Infected DFU requiring frequent inspection. Ischaemic limb. Heavily exuding ulcers requiring daily dressing changes.

THS_021.name: Removable Offloading Devices (Walker / Healing Sandal)
THS_021.indication: Removable offloading when non-removable is contraindicated, not tolerated, or operationally impractical.
THS_021.contraindications: None absolute \u2014 but non-removable preferred when possible.

THS_022.name: Heel Offloading / Suspension Devices
THS_022.indication: Devices offloading the heel or floating the limb to reduce pressure and shear. For heel pressure injuries or fragile posterior heel tissue.
THS_022.guidelines: NPIAP Pressure Injury Prevention/Treatment; EPUAP/NPIAP CPG

THS_023.name: Pressure Redistribution Support Surfaces
THS_023.indication: Specialised mattresses, overlays, cushions (alternating pressure, low-air-loss, reactive foam) redistributing interface pressure to prevent/treat PU.

therapy.rationale: Hydrogel dressings donate moisture to the lightly exuding, necrotic wound bed, facilitating autolytic debridement as recommended by WHS and EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA guidelines. A secondary foam cover protects the wound and manages fluid. A pressure redistribution support surface is critical to mitigate the mechanical forces causing the sacral pressure injury.

For deep pressure injuries with necrosis or slough, it emphasizes individualized care plans, including nutritional optimization with high-calorie, high-protein supplements. Prophylactic dressings and appropriate support surfaces are recommended to manage mechanical loads and protect skin integrity.

sources.title: Wound Dressings for Managing Pressure Injuries
sources.relevance_reasoning: Systematic clinical evidence assessment evaluating the efficacy of advanced wound dressings for pressure injuries.
sources.summary: Advanced wound dressings, including foam, hydrocolloid, alginate, and hydrogel, are recommended over basic gauze to promote a moist wound environment and facilitate pressure injury healing. While evidence suggests advanced dressings are more effective than basic gauze, no single advanced dressing type has been proven superior to others. Clinicians should select dressings based on individual wound characteristics, such as exudate level, depth, and infection status, while prioritizing patient comfort and ease of use.

therapy.rationale: For an infected malignant fungating wound with high exudate, silver antimicrobial dressings are used to manage local bioburden and infection. High exudate levels in the head and neck region are managed with superabsorbent polymer dressings for maximum capacity, secured by tubular retention to avoid adhesive trauma on fragile skin. Liquid skin barrier films protect the periwound from maceration caused by excessive fluid.

sources.title: NHS FORTH VALLEY: Guidelines for the Management of Malignant Wounds (M:EMPHIS PATHWAY)
sources.summary: Management of malignant fungating wounds focuses on palliative symptom control, including managing high exudate with absorbent dressings and infection with appropriate antimicrobials.

contraindications: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT) is contraindicated in malignant wounds due to the risk of tumor growth.
Aggressive debridement is avoided due to high bleeding risks in friable malignant tissue.

therapy.rationale: For a superficial, granulating pressure injury on the head and neck with light exudate, a hydrogel primary dressing maintains a moist environment to support epithelialisation. A foam secondary cover provides cushioning and handles minor fluid. Therapeutic support surfaces are essential to redistribute pressure at the site of injury. Liquid skin barrier films protect the delicate periwound skin from moisture and friction.

sources.title: Prevention and Treatment of Pressure Ulcers/Injuries: Clinical Practice Guideline
sources.summary: The guideline recommends selecting moist wound dressings such as hydrogels for non-infected pressure injuries to facilitate healing and using support surfaces to manage mechanical loads.

contraindications: Avoid highly absorbent dressings on lightly exuding wounds to prevent desiccation of new tissue.

therapy.rationale: For a superficial arterial foot ulcer with necrosis and no exudate, povidone-iodine dressings are indicated for wound bed preparation and to keep the site dry. Non-absorbent gauze provides simple protection, while microporous tape ensures a breathable fixation. A removable offloading device is used to redistribute pressure from the foot, and emollients maintain the integrity of the surrounding skin.

sources.title: Dressings and topical agents for arterial leg ulcers
sources.summary: Current evidence suggests a focus on addressing underlying arterial insufficiency, while topical management focuses on infection prevention and maintaining a stable environment.

contraindications: Debridement is contraindicated in the presence of severe ischaemia without infection.
Avoid occlusive dressings when peripheral pulses are absent to prevent further ischaemic damage.

therapy.rationale: For an infected, deep atypical wound with moderate exudate and slough, Cadexomer Iodine is indicated to provide controlled antimicrobial release while absorbing exudate and facilitating debridement. A superabsorbent secondary dressing manages fluid under retention, while barrier creams protect the periwound from maceration.

sources.summary: Management of malignant fungating wounds focuses on symptom control and quality of life rather than healing. For bleeding, the protocol suggests alginate dressings as first-line treatment, with tranexamic acid or silver nitrate as secondary options.

sources.title: Section 14: Management of Malignant Wounds
sources.relevance_reasoning: Official regional wound formulary section dedicated to the symptomatic management of malignant wounds.
sources.summary: For malignant wounds with necrosis, slough, and excessive exudate, the document recommends effective cleansing to disrupt biofilm and the use of antimicrobial agents like honey or PHMB. Management of excessive exudate should involve super-absorbent silicone dressings or wound manager bags, while ensuring trauma-free removal to address pain and bleeding. If infection is present, an antimicrobial dressing should be paired with a super-absorbent secondary dressing.

sources.title: Managing a malignant wound in palliative care

sources.summary: Management of malignant wounds in palliative care focuses on symptom control and quality of life rather than healing. Key interventions include gentle cleansing, the use of absorbent dressings to manage exudate and odour, and systemic analgesia for pain. A holistic, multidisciplinary approach is essential to address the complex physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs of patients with advanced cancer.

contraindications: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT) is contraindicated due to the risk of promoting tumour genesis and metastasis.
Active/sharp debridement is contraindicated due to the high risk of bleeding in friable malignant tissue.

A liquid skin barrier protects the periwound from any moisture buildup.

sources.summary: Abstract: This guideline is a collaborative effort from Partner Organizations, the European Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel (EPUAP), National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP), and Pan Pacific Pressure Injury Alliance (PPPIA), and 14 additional wound organizations around the world. A comprehensive literature review was conducted on pressure injury prevention and treatment and a rigorous methodology was used to appraise the research and make evidence-based recommendations. This work builds on the work of the previous two editions of this guideline (2009 and 2014). Further, an international survey of patient consumers and their informal caregivers was undertaken to capture the perspectives of these individuals in the prevention and treatment of pressure injuries. The research evidence was summarized and evaluated using evidence-to-decision frameworks. Where sufficient research evidence was available, recommendations to guide clinical practice were developed. In areas without sufficient research, good practice statements were developed to promote comprehensive care. Both the recommendations and good practice statements are accompanied by implementation considerations supported by the research and/or expert opinion. The draft recommendations were made available to stakeholders for feedback. There were 699 health professionals, industry representatives, peak body organizations, researchers, policy makers, patient consumers and informal caregivers who reviewed and/or commented on the document. After refining the content, the final stage of the guideline development consisted of a consensus voting process to assign strengths of recommendations. Strength of recommendations indicate the extent to which one can be confident that adherence to a recommendation will do more good than harm, and are intended to assist health professionals to prioritize interventions. The guideline includes discussion of the science, followed by 115 recommendations and 61 good practice statements to guide practice in risk assessment, pressure injury prevention and treatment, and issues in implementing best practice. The needs of specific population groups are discussed, including individuals with obesity, critically ill individuals, older adults, neonates and children, and individuals in palliative care, operating room and community settings. The guideline also discusses the patient perspective of pressure injuries, and covers topics of importance to individuals, including pain and quality of life. Recommendations on supporting and engaging the patient consumer in their care are made. Finally, 20 quality indicators are provided to assist in monitoring implementation of the guideline.

sources.title: Leg ulceration in venous and arteriovenous insufficiency assessment and management with compression therapy as part of a holistic wound-healing strategy
sources.relevance_reasoning: Peer-reviewed international consensus document detailing VLU assessment, compression, and wound bed preparation.
sources.summary: For venous leg ulcers with high exudate and necrosis, the document recommends a holistic approach including wound bed preparation (debridement and infection control) and compression therapy. In cases of combined arterial and venous insufficiency (CAVI), compression must be applied with caution, limiting pressure to a maximum of 40 mmHg after thorough vascular assessment. Inelastic compression systems are generally preferred for their ability to provide high working pressure and effective calf pump support, which aids in managing exudate and promoting healing.

Compression therapy is the gold standard for healing and should be initiated after a vascular assessment (ABPI) confirms safety. For complex ulcers with high exudate, clinicians should select absorbent dressings that effectively contain fluid to prevent maceration, while ensuring the compression system is appropriate for the limb's shape and condition.

sources.relevance_reasoning: A recent, comprehensive clinical evidence assessment summarizing systematic reviews and guidelines on dressings for pressure injuries.
sources.summary: Advanced wound dressings, including foam, hydrocolloid, alginate, and hydrogel, are recommended over basic gauze to promote a moist wound environment and facilitate pressure injury healing. While evidence suggests advanced dressings are more effective than basic gauze, no single advanced dressing type has been proven superior to others. Clinicians should select dressings based on individual wound characteristics, such as exudate level, depth, and infection status, while prioritizing patient comfort and ease of use.
